## Objectives

By the end of this assignment, you will be able to:

- Identify the base case and the recursive case of a problem, and write both
- Trace what the run-time stack is doing while a recursive function runs
- Implement depth-first search with an explicit Stack
- Implement breadth-first search with an explicit Queue, and explain why it
  finds the shortest route when depth-first search does not
- Explain why a cell must be marked visited when it goes into the container
  rather than when it comes out
- Implement the same search recursively, with no container of your own, and say
  what is doing the remembering instead

---

This assignment covers course skills **E1** (identify base case and recursive
case), **E2** (trace the call stack, winding and unwinding) and **E3**
(implement a recursive solution to a moderate problem), from cluster **E**,
assessed at **Window 2** on Nov 20. It also puts both of week 9's containers to
work, against each other, in the same program.

## 1. Introduction

A maze file is a rectangle of characters. `#` is a wall, `.` is open, `S` is
where you start and `E` is where you are trying to get to. From any open square
you can step up, down, left or right, never diagonally. Here is a small one:

```
#########
#S......#
#.#####.#
#.#...#.#
#...#...#
#.#.#####
#.#....E#
#########
```

![The same maze drawn, with the row and column of every square. A square is named by row, then column: `S` is 1,1 and `E` is 6,7.](../../figures/a12-intro-maze.png){#fig-intro-maze fig-alt="The small maze drawn as a grid of dark walls and white open squares, 8 rows by 9 columns, numbered 0 to 7 down the left and 0 to 8 along the top. S is at row 1, column 1, and E at row 6, column 7. Row 1 is open from S across to column 7. Column 1 is open from S down to row 6. Column 7 is open from row 1 down to row 4. Row 4 runs from column 1 to column 3 and from column 5 to column 7, and row 3 runs from column 3 to column 5, so the open squares form a loop around a small block of wall. Column 3 continues down from row 4 to row 6, and row 6 runs from column 3 across to E."}

There are two ways from `S` to `E`. The short one goes down the left side and
along the bottom, 12 squares counting both ends. The long one goes right along
the top, round the loop in the middle and down to the bottom, 22 squares.

You will write three programs that find a route. All three keep a record of
the squares they have already found, and all three need somewhere to keep the
squares they have found but not looked at yet. That somewhere is what makes
them different.

### Depth first, with a Stack (TODO 3)

Push `S` onto a Stack. Then, over and over: pop the top cell, and push each of
its open neighbors that has not been found yet. Stop when `E` comes out.

The first three steps on this maze:

| step | pop | push | the Stack after, top on the right |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1,1 (`S`) | 2,1 and 1,2 | 2,1 · 1,2 |
| 2 | 1,2 | 1,3 | 2,1 · 1,3 |
| 3 | 1,3 | 1,4 | 2,1 · 1,4 |

A Stack hands back the cell pushed last. After step 1 that is 1,2, the square
to the right of `S`, so the search heads right along row 1, and every pop
after that takes the square it has just found. It follows that corridor to
the end, goes round the loop and reaches `E` with the long route, **22
squares**. 2,1, the way down from `S`, sits at the bottom of the Stack the
whole time and is never popped.

### Breadth first, with a Queue (TODO 4)

The same loop with a Queue: `add` where TODO 3 has `push`, `remove` where it
has `pop`.

| step | remove | add | the Queue after, front on the left |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1,1 (`S`) | 2,1 and 1,2 | 2,1 · 1,2 |
| 2 | 2,1 | 3,1 | 1,2 · 3,1 |
| 3 | 1,2 | 1,3 | 3,1 · 1,3 |
| 4 | 3,1 | 4,1 | 1,3 · 4,1 |

A Queue hands back the cell that has waited longest, so the search takes turns:
one square down, one square right, another down, another right. Every square
one step from `S` comes out before any square two steps away, every square two
steps away before any three steps away, and so on. So the first time `E`
comes out, it has come the shortest way: **12 squares**.

### Depth first, recursively (TODO 5)

No container of your own. A function `explore(cell)` adds the cell to the
path and calls itself on each neighbor that has not been found yet. If one of
those calls reaches `E`, it is done. If none of them does, it takes its cell
back off the path and returns `false`.

`explore` tries the neighbors in the order up, down, left, right, so from `S`
it goes down first. At 6,1 it hits a dead end: `explore(6,1)` and then
`explore(5,1)` return `false`, and both squares come back off the path. From
4,1 it goes right to 4,3, then up and all the way round the loop, until it
reaches 1,2, next to `S`, where every neighbor has been found. Fourteen calls
return `false` one after another, back to 4,3. From 4,3 it goes down and
reaches `E`: **12 squares**.

Each call that is still waiting for an answer is a frame on the run-time
stack, and at every moment those frames are exactly the squares on the path.
That is the stack this version uses, without declaring one.

### All three at once

![The three searches on this maze, one step at a time. The Stack and the Queue take two frames per step: a cell comes out (it rises out of the row of boxes and turns gold in the maze), then its neighbors go in (outlined boxes). The recursive search takes one frame per call or return, and its row of boxes is the run-time stack, one box per call of `explore`.](../../figures/a12-intro-search.gif){#fig-intro-search fig-alt="An animation in three rows, one per search, each with the small maze on the left and its container drawn as a row of boxes labeled row,col on the right. Row one, depth first with a Stack: the Stack's top is its right end; the search runs right along row 1, round the loop and down to E, and ends with a 22-square route while 2,1 is still waiting in the Stack. Row two, breadth first with a Queue: cells leave from the front on the left and join at the back on the right; the search spreads down and right in turn and ends with the 12-square route down the left side and along the bottom. Row three, depth first recursively: the boxes are the run-time stack, one per call of explore, newest on the right, and a thin line in the maze joins the squares on the path. It goes down to the dead end at 6,1 and backs out, goes round the loop and backs out of all of it one call at a time, then goes down from 4,3 to E, ending with the 12-square route as twelve frames."}

| | remembers with | route on this maze | promises |
|---|---|---|---|
| **depth first** | a `Stack` | 22 squares | *a* route |
| **breadth first** | a `Queue` | 12 squares | the **shortest** route |
| **depth first, recursively** | the run-time stack | 12 squares | *a* route |

The two depth-first versions both follow one corridor as far as it goes, but
they try the neighbors in opposite orders. The Stack pops the neighbor pushed
last, which is the one to the right. `explore` tries the first one in the
list, up, then down. That is the only reason the recursive version found the
short route here. On another maze the order can work against it. Only the Queue
finds the shortest route on every maze.

This maze is in your repository as `mazes/loop.txt`. Once your solvers work,
`./a12 mazes/loop.txt` should print 22, 12 and 12. The other mazes are bigger.
On `mazes/twoways.txt` the Stack's route is 89 squares and the Queue's is 29.

::: {.callout-note}
**This is a search problem, and searching is one of the main jobs these
containers do.** Route-finding, solving a puzzle, working out which packages a
package depends on, finding the shortest chain of friends between two people,
a compiler deciding what to rebuild: each of these is this program with
something else in place of the maze.
:::

## 3. What You Were Given

**You edit one file: `Solver.cpp`.** Five TODOs.

| File | Yours? | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `Solver.cpp` | **yes** | TODOs 1–5 |
| `Solver.h` | no | the specification. Read this first. |
| `Maze.h`, `Maze.cpp` | no | the maze, and two helpers you should use |
| `Stack.h`, `Queue.h` | **replaceable** | working containers, see below |
| `main.cpp` | no | solves a maze three ways and draws the results |
| `mazes/` | no | eight mazes |
| `checks.cpp` | no | the course's checks |

### Two helpers you should use

`Maze.h` ends with two functions that are given to you because they are fiddly
and are not what this assignment is about:

- **`openNeighbours(maze, cell)`**, the open cells next to `cell`, in a fixed
  order: up, down, left, right. Walls and cells off the edge of the maze are
  left out, so your solvers never check the boundaries themselves. The order is
  fixed on purpose: it is what makes depth-first search produce the same answer
  on every machine.
- **`retrace(maze, parent)`**, turns a grid of parents into a `Path`. §5
  explains what that means.

### `Stack.h` and `Queue.h`

The ones in the repository work, and they are **not the a10 answer key**. They
are thin shells around `std::vector` and `std::deque`, no array, no `mySize`,
nothing circular. They give nothing away about a10. You only need their method
names, which are a10's: `push`, `pop` and `isEmpty` for the Stack, `add`,
`remove` and `isEmpty` for the Queue.

If your own a10 containers work, copy your `Stack.h` and `Queue.h` over these
and everything will keep compiling: same class, same methods, same exceptions.
It is a good feeling to watch `Stack<Cell>` just work on a type you had never
heard of when you wrote it.

::: {.callout-note}
**Grading always uses the shipped containers, whatever you leave in those
files.** So dropping in your own cannot help your a12 score and a bug in them
cannot hurt it. a12 grades your search. a10 already graded your containers,
and one rough week should not cost you two.
:::

## 4. TODOs 1 and 2, two recursive warm-ups {#warm-ups}

Before any maze, two small functions. Both must be **recursive**, and neither
may contain a `for` or a `while`. There are checks that read your source, so a
loop will not slip past, but the real reason is that Wednesday's lecture is
about what the run-time stack does while these run, and a loop does not do it.

Every recursive function is the same two questions:

> **the base case**, what is so small that the answer is obvious?
>
> **the recursive case**, how do I make the problem one step smaller, and what
> do I do with the answer to the smaller problem?

**TODO 1, `sumArray(values, n)`**, the sum of the first `n` elements.

The base case is `n == 0`: the sum of no numbers is 0.

Trace it for `{5, 3, 8}` before you write it:

```
  sumArray(v, 3)  needs  sumArray(v, 2)  +  v[2]
    sumArray(v, 2)  needs  sumArray(v, 1)  +  v[1]      ← winding
      sumArray(v, 1)  needs  sumArray(v, 0)  +  v[0]
        sumArray(v, 0)  =  0                            ← the base case
      sumArray(v, 1)  =  0 + 5   =  5
    sumArray(v, 2)  =  5 + 3   =  8                     ← unwinding
  sumArray(v, 3)  =  8 + 8   =  16
```

Going down is the **winding** phase, and coming back up is **unwinding**.
Both are on Wednesday's slides, and they are much easier to see on a
three-element array than on a maze.

**TODO 2, `reverseArray(values, n)`**, in place.

Swap the two ends, then the middle is a smaller version of the same problem.
`&values[1]` is the array starting one element later, the same `&a[1]` as the
`sum` slide on Monday, and it is how you hand the middle to the next call.

::: {.callout-warning}
Count carefully. If you swap the two ends of an `n`-element array, the middle
has **n − 2** elements left in it, not n − 1. Getting that wrong gives you an
array that is reversed almost everywhere.
:::

## 5. The search, before either container {#the-search}

All three solvers do the same three things. Read this once before writing any
of them. After this section TODO 3 is mostly typing.

### Two grids beside the maze

```cpp
vector<vector<bool>> visited(maze.getRows(), vector<bool>(maze.getCols(), false));
vector<vector<Cell>> parent(maze.getRows(),  vector<Cell>(maze.getCols()));
```

`visited[r][c]`, have I already discovered this cell?
`parent[r][c]`, which cell was I standing on when I discovered it?

Copy those two lines as they are. They are new, so read them from the inside
out:

- `vector<bool>(maze.getCols(), false)` is **one row**: a vector of
  `getCols()` items, every one of them `false`.
- `vector<vector<bool>> visited(maze.getRows(), ...)` is a vector whose items
  are rows, `getRows()` copies of that row.

So `visited[r]` is row `r`, and `visited[r][c]` is the bool in row `r`,
column `c`, the same indexing as the 2D arrays from week 2. `parent` is the
same with `Cell` in place of `bool`, and every `Cell` in it starts as `Cell()`,
which is (0, 0).

Why not a plain 2D array, `bool visited[rows][cols]`? C++ wants an array's
size fixed when the program is compiled, and a maze's size is only known once
its file has been read. A vector can be given its size while the program
runs.

::: {.callout-note}
**No hash table here, and that is a deliberate choice.** A cell *is* a pair of
indices, and the grid is bounded, so an array indexed by `[r][c]` goes straight
to the right slot with no hashing at all. a11's hash function existed to
manufacture a number out of a word, because a word is not a number. A cell
already is one. Adding a hash table would be work that buys nothing.
:::

### The parents grid is how you get a path out

The search visits cells in some order that has nothing to do with the route.
What turns that into a route is the `parent` grid: each cell remembers who
discovered it, so from the end you can walk backwards to the start.

```
   discovered from        so the parents point back this way
   ─────────────────      ──────────────────────────────────
     S → a → b → c            S ← a ← b ← c
         ↘ d → E                  ↖ d ← E
```

Start at `E`, follow the arrows to `S`, and turn the list around. That is
exactly what `retrace(maze, parent)` does, you record the parents, and it does
the walk. It needs one thing from you: **the start's parent must be the start
itself**, because that is how it knows where to stop.

### The one mistake everybody makes {#mark-on-the-way-in}

> **Mark a cell visited when you PUT IT IN the container, not when you take it
> out.**

Here is the difference, on one cell with three unvisited neighbors:

```
mark on the way IN                    mark on the way OUT

  pop A                                 pop A, mark A
  look at b, c, d                       look at b, c, d
    b unmarked → mark it, push it         b unmarked → push it
    c unmarked → mark it, push it         c unmarked → push it
    d unmarked → mark it, push it         d unmarked → push it
                                        ...later, pop b, mark b
  container: b c d                        look at b's neighbors, which
  each cell enters exactly once            include c and d, still unmarked,
                                           so push both AGAIN
                                        container: c d c d ...
```

Each cell going in exactly once is what makes a capacity of rows × cols the
right size, and it is what makes the parent you record **the first way anybody
found that cell**.

::: {.callout-important}
**With the Stack, marking on the way out is merely wasteful.** Cells go in
several times, get expanded several times, and you still get a valid path out
of the other end. Slower, but not wrong.

**With the Queue it is fatal.** Breadth-first search expands an entire ring of
cells before it takes any of them back out, so the duplicates pile up instead
of being consumed: the queue overruns the capacity you gave it, and a cell's
parent can be overwritten by a *longer* route before it is ever removed. There
goes the shortest path, which was the only reason to use a Queue.
:::

## 6. TODO 3, depth first, with a Stack

```
make visited and parent, both the size of the maze
make a Stack<Cell> with room for rows * cols cells
mark the start visited, make it its own parent, push it

while the stack is not empty:
    pop a cell
    if it is the end:  return retrace(maze, parent)
    for each cell in openNeighbours(maze, that cell):
        if it has not been visited:
            mark it visited
            record the cell you came from as its parent
            push it

return an empty Path        // the stack ran dry without reaching the end
```

An empty `Path` is an answer, not a failure. `mazes/nopath.txt` has no route
through it and all three of your solvers have to say so cleanly.

This is the longest of the three. Get it working on `mazes/tiny.txt`, three
cells in a row, before you point it at anything larger.

## 7. TODO 4, breadth first, with a Queue {#breadth-first}

Copy TODO 3. Change three things:

```
Stack<Cell>  →  Queue<Cell>
push         →  add
pop          →  remove
```

That is the entire difference. Same visited grid, same parents, same loop.

And the answer changes completely:

```bash
./a12 mazes/room.txt
```

```
  depth first (Stack)      breadth first (Queue)
  ###############          ###############
  #S************#          #S............#
  #............*#          #*............#
  #*************#          #*............#
  #*............#          #*............#
  #*************#          #*............#
  #............E#          #************E#
  ###############          ###############

  42 cells                 18 cells
```

### Why changing the container does that

![`mazes/twoways.txt`, both searches side by side, one step at a time. Each step takes one cell out of the container (it rises out of the row of boxes and turns gold in the maze), then puts its unvisited neighbors in (the outlined boxes). The boxes are labeled with each cell's row and column.](../../figures/a12-maze-search.gif){#fig-maze-search fig-alt="An animation of the twoways maze drawn twice, side by side, with row and column numbers along the edges. On the left, depth-first search with a Stack; on the right, breadth-first search with a Queue. Under each maze the container is drawn as a row of boxes labeled row,col: the Stack's top is its right end, and the Queue's front is its left end and its back its right end. Each step, one box rises out of the container and that cell turns gold in the maze, then the cell's unvisited neighbors join the container as outlined boxes and turn light gold in the maze. Cells already taken out are pink. The Stack runs down one corridor at a time and reaches E after taking out 95 cells, with a winding route of 89 cells drawn in maroon and 13 cells left in the Stack, never needed. The Queue spreads out evenly across the maze and reaches E after taking out all 129 open cells, with a route of 29 cells."}

A container decides **what you look at next**, and that is the only decision a
search makes.

A **Stack** hands back the most recent thing you put in. So you always continue
from the cell you just discovered: you commit to one direction and follow it as
far as it goes, only backing up when you hit a dead end. Deep first. When it
finally stumbles into the end, the route it took is whatever wandering got it
there.

A **Queue** hands back the oldest thing you put in. So you finish every cell one
step from the start before you look at anything two steps away, and every cell
two steps away before anything three steps away. The search spreads out in
rings:

```
        3 3 3 3 3
        3 2 2 2 3          the ring of cells at distance 2 is
        3 2 1 2 3          entirely finished before any cell at
        3 2 1 S 3          distance 3 is looked at
        3 3 3 3 3
```

The first time the end is discovered, it is discovered from the smallest ring
that touches it. There is no shorter way in, because a shorter way would have
been in an earlier ring, and the earlier rings are already done.

That is the guarantee, and it comes entirely from the order the container
gives things back. Neither search knows anything the other does not.

::: {.callout-warning}
Breadth-first search cannot be *longer* than depth-first search. If `./a12`
tells you it is, something in TODO 4 is still behaving like TODO 3, most
likely the container.
:::

## 8. TODO 5, depth first, with no container {#recursively}

Same search. No `Stack`.

You will want a helper that calls itself:

```cpp
bool explore(const Maze& maze, Cell here,
             vector<vector<bool>>& visited, Path& path);
```

which returns `true` if the end can be reached from `here`, and leaves the route
from `here` onwards on the back of `path`. Write it in `Solver.cpp` **above**
`solveRecursively`, so the compiler has seen it by the time
`solveRecursively` calls it. `path.push_back(here)` adds a cell to the back of
the path and `path.pop_back()` takes it off again, the vector methods from
week 5.

```
mark here visited
add here to the path
if here is the end:  return true
for each unvisited cell in openNeighbours(maze, here):
    if explore(maze, that cell, visited, path):  return true
take here back off the end of the path        ← do not forget this
return false
```

::: {.callout-important}
**Do not leave out that second-to-last line.** When a branch turns out to be a dead end, the cells you walked down
it are not part of the answer and have to come back off. Leave them on and you
get a "path" that teleports, and the checks will tell you so, because two cells
in a row on it stop being next to each other.
:::

Note what you do **not** undo: `visited`. A cell that led nowhere still leads
nowhere the second time. Un-marking it turns a fast search into one that
explores every route in the maze separately.

### What is doing the remembering

There is no `Stack<Cell>` in this version, and yet the search still backs up out
of dead ends and carries on where it left off. Something is keeping track.

It is the **run-time stack**, Wednesday's lecture. Every call to `explore` gets
its own frame holding its own `here` and its own position in the neighbor loop,
stacked on top of the caller's. When a call returns, its frame is thrown away
and the one underneath picks up exactly where it stopped.

That is the same discipline you implemented by hand in TODO 3: last in, first
out. In TODO 3 you allocated the storage and pushed and popped it yourself. Here
the compiler does it, in the same shape, for free.

::: {.callout-note}
**And that is also this version's limitation.** Its depth is bounded by how much
run-time stack the program has, which is not something you control. On these
mazes it is nowhere near a problem. On a maze of a million cells it would be,
and TODO 3 would still work, because a `Stack<Cell>` lives in the heap, where
there is room.
:::

## 9. Testing Your Work

```bash
make test         # all 32 checks
```

::: {.callout-important}
**There are no hidden tests.** What you run with `make test` is exactly what the
grader runs, all 32 checks, every one of them in a file in your repository.
:::

| | |
|---|---|
| 7 | the two warm-ups |
| 7 | depth first, with a Stack |
| 4 | breadth first, with a Queue |
| 6 | the recursive solver, and where all three must agree |
| 5 | your source: which container each one uses, and what is recursive |
| 3 | twelve mazes generated while you are being graded |

::: {.callout-note}
**Nothing compares your path against a stored answer.** Most of these mazes have
more than one route, and depth-first search may find any of them, so a path is
checked against the definition instead: starts at `S`, ends at `E`, every cell
open, consecutive cells adjacent, no repeats.

Breadth-first search gets one extra requirement, its **length**, and even that
is measured against a shortest distance the checks compute for themselves, so
any shortest route will do.
:::

Each check runs in its own process. A recursive function with no reachable base
case is killed when it runs out of stack, and because each check runs alone,
that costs you one check rather than the whole run.

Run one on its own while you are debugging:

```bash
make checks
./checks "Stack: it finds a valid path through room"
```

```bash
./a12 mazes/twisty.txt
```

`twisty.txt` is a **perfect maze**: exactly one route between any two cells.
All three of your solvers return the same 157 cells, because there is nothing
for them to disagree about.

Then run `mazes/room.txt` again, where there are thousands of routes and the
three answers share almost no cells at all.

When there is only one answer, the container you use does not matter. When
there are many, the container decides which one you get.
:::
